title: Phrasal Verbs in Professional and Social Life
learningObjectives: Master phrasal verbs used in professional environments
Understand phrasal verbs in social and informal contexts
Learn to distinguish between literal and figurative meanings
Practice using phrasal verbs in complex sentences

sections.title: Phrasal Verbs at the Intermediate Level
sections.content: At the B1 level, you need phrasal verbs for more complex situations — at work, in social life, and when discussing plans. Many phrasal verbs have multiple meanings depending on context. Understanding these will make your English sound much more natural and fluent.

sections.title: In the Workplace
sections.content:
Modern workplaces are full of phrasal verbs. The team needs to <come up with> a strategy. The manager asks everyone to <think it over>. They <bring up> ideas and <talk them through>. Some are <turned down>, but they <end up> choosing a creative approach.

• <Come up with> - create/invent an idea
• <Think over> - consider carefully
• <Bring up> - mention a topic
• <Turn down> - reject
• <End up> - finally arrive at a result
• <Get on with> - continue doing

sections.title: Social Situations
sections.content:
Phrasal verbs are essential in social English:

I was supposed to meet my friend, but she <called off> our plans. I decided to <hang out> with others instead. The food really <lived up to> the reviews. We <caught up> on each other's news.

• <Call off> - cancel
• <Hang out> - spend time casually
• <Live up to> - meet expectations
• <Catch up> - exchange recent news
• <Get along with> - have a good relationship

sections.title: Multiple Meanings
sections.content:
Example 1: PICK UP - <Pick up the phone (answer) / Pick up a language (learn informally) / Pick up someone (collect by car)>

Example 2: TAKE OFF - <The plane took off (left the ground) / Take off your coat (remove) / Her career took off (became successful)>

Example 3: WORK OUT - <I work out at the gym (exercise) / Things worked out well (had a good result) / Work out the answer (calculate)>

sections.title: Travel and Leisure
sections.content:
Phrasal verbs for travel and free time:

• <Look into> - Research or investigate destinations
• <Set off> - Begin a journey
• <Check in/out> - Register arrival/departure at a hotel
• <Get around> - Travel within an area
• <Eat out> - Have a meal at a restaurant
• <Get back> - Return to a place

Example: <Look into> flights before booking. <Set off> early to avoid traffic. <Get around> by public transport.

sections.title: Emotions and Reactions
sections.content:
Many phrasal verbs describe how we feel and react:

• <Cheer up> - Become happier or make someone happier
• <Calm down> - Become less angry or excited
• <Open up> - Start to talk about your feelings
• <Bottle up> - Keep your feelings hidden inside
• <Let down> - Disappoint someone
• <Look up to> - Admire and respect someone
• <Put up with> - Tolerate something unpleasant

Example: Her friends <cheered her up>. She <opened up> about her worries and felt better.

sections.title: Phrasal Verbs in Conversations
sections.content:
Example 1: PLANNING A TRIP - <We should look into flights to Barcelona. Let's set off early on Friday.>

Example 2: EMOTIONAL SUPPORT - <A: You seem stressed.
B: My boss let me down again. I've been bottling up my feelings.
A: You shouldn't put up with it — speak to HR.>

Example 3: WEEKEND - <A: What did you get up to this weekend?
B: We ate out on Saturday and hung out at the park on Sunday.>

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
Remember:

• Context determines the meaning of phrasal verbs with multiple definitions
• Professional English uses many phrasal verbs — learn them for career growth
• Social phrasal verbs make you sound natural in conversations
• Practice by reading articles and noting phrasal verbs you find
• Try to use at least one new phrasal verb each day in conversation

keyVocabulary.definition: To think of an idea or plan
keyVocabulary.example: We need to come up with a solution.
Let me think it over before I decide.

keyVocabulary.definition: To mention a topic in conversation
keyVocabulary.example: She brought up an interesting point.

keyVocabulary.definition: To reject an offer or request
keyVocabulary.example: He turned down the job offer.

keyVocabulary.definition: To cancel an event or arrangement
To exchange recent news with someone
keyVocabulary.example: Let's meet for coffee and catch up.
The movie didn't live up to the hype.
Let's get on with the project.

grammarPoints.explanation: Many common phrasal verbs have 2-3 different meanings.
examples: The plane took off. (= left the ground)
commonMistakes: Using the wrong meaning in context: 'I need to work out the gym' — Wrong! Say 'I need to work out at the gym'
